big_idea: Some events CAN'T happen (impossible). Some MIGHT (possible). Some MUST (certain).
learning_intention: We are learning to name events as impossible, possible, or certain.
student_learning_goal: I can name events as impossible, possible, or certain.
success_criteria: I can name an event as IMPOSSIBLE.
I can name an event as POSSIBLE.
I can name an event as CERTAIN.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Lucky and Mae — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 1 likelihood tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Lucky: WILL the sun fly to the moon today? IMPOSSIBLE! WILL it rain at recess? POSSIBLE! WILL the day end? CERTAIN!
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lucky and Mae puppets. 'Friends — I'm Lucky Lou the Loon, and this is Maybe Mae the Cat. Today we learn 3 BIG words about LIKELIHOOD: IMPOSSIBLE, POSSIBLE, CERTAIN.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write IMPOSSIBLE, POSSIBLE, CERTAIN on chart. 'Impossible = it CANNOT happen. Possible = it MIGHT happen. Certain = it WILL happen for sure.'

Demonstrate. Hold up event cards one at a time:
- 'A pig will fly today.' (IMPOSSIBLE — pigs cannot fly.)
- 'It will snow in July in Toronto.' (IMPOSSIBLE.)
- 'It will rain at recess.' (POSSIBLE — might or might not.)
- 'I will eat lunch today.' (CERTAIN — yes.)
- 'The sun will rise tomorrow.' (CERTAIN.)
- 'I will see a unicorn at recess.' (IMPOSSIBLE.)
- 'A friend will smile at me today.' (POSSIBLE — likely!)

More Canadian-flavour examples:
- 'Maple leaves fall in fall.' (CERTAIN.)
- 'Snow in July.' (IMPOSSIBLE.)
- 'Rain at recess.' (POSSIBLE.)
- 'A coin lands on heads.' (POSSIBLE.)

'Lucky says — every event fits ONE of these three. Decide impossible / possible / certain.'

'Today YOU sort lots of events.'
student_actions: Decide events as impossible / possible / certain.

steps.instruction: Whole group: name 6 events as I/P/C. Use Canadian examples (snow in July, rain in spring, maple leaves fall, etc.).
Three stations. Station A: Sort 8 'impossible' event cards. Station B: Sort 8 'possible' event cards. Station C: Sort 8 'certain' event cards.
Stretch challenge at Station C: write your own EVENT CARD and decide its likelihood.
Discuss the 3 categories. 'Impossible has NO chance. Certain has ALL chance. Possible is in between.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show with hand gestures: closed fist (no), open palm (yes), middle hand (maybe).

steps.instruction: Circulate to record diagnostic evidence on the likelihood tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Why is this impossible?' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only obvious 'impossible' events.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: invent 3 events for each category.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use a sentence frame: 'This is ___ because ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children physically move to one of 3 corners (impossible / possible / certain) when teacher names an event.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: names IMPOSSIBLE; names POSSIBLE; names CERTAIN.

consolidation.exit_routine: Each child names ONE example of each: 'Impossible: ___. Possible: ___. Certain: ___.'

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 surfaces children who already use likelihood vocabulary from those who only know 'maybe'.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says POSSIBLE for everything — repairing the all-possible default at Grade 1
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-1 trap on D2.1 is the all-possible default: the child assigns POSSIBLE to almost every event because 'it could happen, right?'. They miss that some events are TRULY impossible (pigs flying) and some are TRULY certain (sun rising tomorrow).

This matters because likelihood requires distinguishing between three real categories. The default 'possible' collapses the distinction.

The walkthrough covers when a child labels everything possible.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Card: 'A horse will sit on my chair.' Child says 'POSSIBLE'. Card: 'Sun rises tomorrow.' Child says 'POSSIBLE'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You said both POSSIBLE. But Lucky says — there are 3 different words.'

Walk through. 'Card 1: A horse sits on your chair. Could that REALLY happen here today? No — a horse won't fit, won't be brought to school. That's IMPOSSIBLE.'

'Card 2: Sun rises tomorrow. Has it ALWAYS risen? Yes. Will it tomorrow? Yes — that's CERTAIN.'

Generalise. 'Lucky says — IMPOSSIBLE means NEVER. CERTAIN means ALWAYS. POSSIBLE is the middle — sometimes yes, sometimes no.'

Now practice. 'A snowman will be in our classroom this afternoon.' Impossible (won't be brought in). 'Lunch will happen today.' Certain. 'It will rain.' Possible.

If still always-possible: provide the 3-term mat. 'Place each card on the right zone.' Force category use.

Long-term recovery: every event activity asks 'never, always, or sometimes?'
expected_student_responses: (Mid) Distinguishes with prompts; uses 'never/always' as bridge.
(Stretched) Gives reasons: 'impossible because pigs cannot fly'.
common_misconceptions: Impossible only means 'silly'. (Repair: impossible means NEVER.)
Certain only means 'today'. (Repair: certain means ALWAYS.)
recovery_moves: Provide many obvious-impossible and obvious-certain cards before mixing in possible.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of D2.1 likelihood term identification.

parts_outline.task: Read 6 events. Circle I (impossible), P (possible), or C (certain).
Sort 6 events into 3 columns: Impossible, Possible, Certain.
Write your own event for each likelihood. 3 events total.
